planting.note: Plant corms 4-6 inches deep in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil, ideally before flowers emerge leafless from bare ground.

directions: Set corms 4-6 inches deep and about 6-9 inches apart in a sunny to lightly shaded bed with rich, well-drained soil, planting in late summer so goblet-shaped flowers appear on bare stems weeks later. Broad strap-like leaves emerge the following spring, photosynthesize, then die back well before the naked blooms return in autumn. The large rosy-lilac flowers are showier than common autumn crocus and work well naturalized under deciduous shrubs or in a rock garden. All parts are toxic if ingested, so site away from grazing animals and small children.

planting.note: Plant corms 4-6 inches deep in late summer, well before the leafless flower spikes push up in early autumn.

directions: Plant the large corms 4-6 inches deep and roughly 6-9 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil during late summer dormancy, choosing a spot that gets sun to light shade. Each corm produces an unusually high number of crocus-like lilac-pink blooms that open directly from the soil without foliage, followed the next spring by large cabbage-like leaves that must be left to die back naturally. It is one of the most floriferous colchicums and naturalizes readily in turf, borders, or woodland edges for a burst of unexpected fall color. Because the foliage and corms are toxic, keep it away from areas where pets or livestock graze.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil so they can flower at the earliest thaw.

directions: Plant small corms 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in a well-drained, sunny site, since standing winter moisture is the main cause of rot. This species blooms even earlier than common Dutch crocus, often pushing through late snow to open cup-shaped flowers in shades of gold, cream, and blue-purple, frequently with contrasting feathered markings. Its grassy foliage is inconspicuous and disappears quickly after bloom, making it ideal for tucking into lawns, rock gardens, and the front of borders. The early nectar is an important first food source for emerging bees.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil, unlike most crocus which prefer drier sites.

directions: Set corms 3-4 inches deep and about 3-4 inches apart in humus-rich soil that holds more moisture than a typical crocus bed, in light woodland shade or a partially shaded border. Unusual among crocuses for its lilac-lavender, iris-like flowers with three enlarged, deeply fringed inner petals, it blooms in autumn alongside its narrow grass-like leaves rather than before them. It is well suited to naturalizing at the edge of woodland gardens or beneath deciduous shrubs where soil stays cool and slightly damp. Established clumps slowly form drifts and provide a distinctive late-season nectar source for pollinators.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, gritty soil to help them survive summer dormancy.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in a sunny, sharply drained spot, since this dwarf iris is prone to rot in soil that stays wet through summer dormancy. It opens bright egg-yolk yellow flowers with darker spotting on the falls, often before its four-sided grassy leaves fully lengthen, making it one of the very earliest bulbs to bloom alongside snowdrops and winter aconite. The blooms are small enough to enjoy up close in rock gardens, troughs, or the front of a raised bed. Bulbs frequently split into non-flowering offsets after the first year, so gardeners often replant fresh bulbs for reliable repeat bloom.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep after danger of frost has passed once soil has warmed in spring.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 8-12 inches apart after the last spring frost in fertile, well-drained soil, choosing a sheltered spot since the tall flower spikes can catch wind. Strap-shaped bluish-green leaves rise first, followed in late summer by arching racemes of pendulous, fragrant white bell flowers reminiscent of giant hyacinths or summer-blooming galtonia relatives. It combines well toward the back of a mixed border or among ornamental grasses, and the cut flower spikes hold up well in arrangements. In climates colder than about zone 7, lift and store the bulbs indoors over winter as you would gladiolus or dahlias.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in late summer in a hot, dry, sun-baked site that mimics its Mediterranean habitat.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in late summer in a hot, sharply drained bed against a south-facing wall or rock garden slope, since this species needs a thorough summer baking to flower well. Large crocus-shaped, bright golden-yellow blooms appear directly from bare soil in autumn, usually just ahead of or alongside the narrow gray-green leaves. It is a choice bulb for a dry Mediterranean-style border, gravel garden, or bulb frame where winter wet can be avoided. Established clumps are best left undisturbed for years, as sternbergias resent frequent lifting and division.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in average, well-drained garden soil for reliable spring bloom and naturalizing.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in ordinary, well-drained soil in a sunny to partly shaded location. Dense spikes of tightly packed, deep blue-violet, urn-shaped flowers with a faint musky-sweet fragrance appear in mid-spring above narrow grassy foliage, and the crowded flower heads give it a slightly darker, more compact look than common grape hyacinths. It self-seeds and multiplies readily by offsets, making it a dependable choice for naturalizing under trees, along paths, or at the front of a spring bulb border. Foliage yellows and can be cut back once it withers in early summer.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil where they can naturalize undisturbed for years.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, positioning them where they will not be disturbed since they resent transplanting once established. Pale silvery-blue, star-shaped flowers with a darker central stripe on each petal open in very early spring, often emerging alongside the last snowdrops and before most other squills. The short flower stalks and low grassy foliage make it a good choice for rock gardens, bulb lawns, or the front edge of a border where early color is welcome. Left undisturbed, it slowly forms dense, long-lived colonies.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun where broad foliage can be displayed.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep and 8-10 inches apart in fall in full sun and well-drained soil, giving each bulb room since it produces unusually broad, wavy-edged, gray-green strap leaves that lie close to the ground. In late spring a stout stalk rises just above the foliage to open a dense, softball-sized umbel of dusty pink to lilac starry florets that dries attractively and holds its shape for weeks. Its low, wide habit makes it a striking edger or front-of-border accent quite different from the tall, leafless-stemmed look of most ornamental onions. The foliage begins to fade around bloom time, so pair it with later-emerging perennials to hide the dying leaves.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil where clumps can be left undisturbed to naturalize.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in a sunny site with sharp drainage, since unlike hybrid tulips this species performs best when left in the ground for years rather than lifted annually. Each bulb sends up several low, sprawling stems that each open into a cheerful star-shaped flower with bright yellow centers and white-tipped petals, several blooms opening together from a single clump. Its compact, spreading habit suits rock gardens, gravel beds, and the front of a sunny border far better than a formal tulip bed. Given good drainage, it reliably returns and slowly multiplies, unlike many modern tulip hybrids that decline after the first season.
